title: Queen Victoria Mourns Prince Albert
text:
Queen Victoria married her cousin, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, in 1840. They had nine children. Albert became her closest adviser, her private secretary in all but name, and the organizer of the Great Exhibition of 1851. She depended on him completely.

In late 1861 Albert, overworked and in poor health, was distressed to learn that their eldest son, the Prince of Wales, had had an affair with an actress. He traveled to Cambridge to speak with his son, walking with him in the rain. Soon afterwards he fell ill with what his doctors diagnosed as typhoid fever. He died at Windsor Castle on 14 December 1861, at forty-two. Victoria never fully forgave her son, whom she partly blamed.

Victoria was forty-two too. She wore black for the rest of her life, nearly forty years. For years she withdrew from public life, and newspapers and politicians grew impatient with her absence. She had Albert's rooms kept as they had been, with his clothes laid out and hot water brought each morning. She raised monuments to him across the country, among them the Albert Memorial and the Royal Albert Hall in London.

In her letters she wrote of being cut off from her husband, and in old age she still marked the anniversary of his death. She lived until 1901, the longest reign in British history until then.
lesson: Grief for a spouse can last a lifetime and shape everything after. Mourning deeply is natural, but those still living, including our children, need us too.
people: Queen Victoria, Prince Albert, Albert Edward, Prince of Wales
source: The Letters of Queen Victoria; Stanley Weintraub, Uncrowned King: The Life of Prince Albert (1997)
caveat: Modern historians debate whether Albert died of typhoid or of a chronic illness such as Crohn's disease.
